## Kathāvatthupakaraṇa-Mūlaṭīkā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Explanation of the Introduction to the Text
By the phrase "kathānaṃ vatthubhāvato" (as the basis of the discourses), it is meant that this treatise, being a collection of discourses, serves as the locus for its own constituent parts (the individual discourses). Indeed, the parts are contained within the whole. To show the manner in which it was taught in brief, it is said: "established only by the setting down of the matrix (mātikā)."

## Explanation of the Narrative (Nidānakathā)
In the phrase "attained Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without residue (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu)," the term Parinibbāna itself is expressed in the instrumental sense (as a cause) to distinguish it from the other Parinibbāna, which is the Nibbāna with residue (saupādisesa-nibbāna). Alternatively, it means that because that Nibbāna element was attained, the final consciousness arose without further rebirth; thus, that Nibbāna element is stated as the cause for the cessation of further rebirth.

Regarding the phrase "having a weak side," it is said to mean a king who rules only a single region (ekamaṇḍalika), rather than a powerful one like King Kālāśoka. However, it is also said to be "weak" because of the absence of wisdom capable of producing the distinction between those who speak according to the Dhamma (dhammavādī) and those who speak against the Dhamma (adhammavādī).

"Of those very persons" refers only to the members of the Bāhuliya sect; they are also known by the name Bahussutika. "The schismatics" (bhinnakā) refers to those who split from the original recital (Mūlasaṅgīti) or the original school (Mūlanikāya). The meaning is that they reached a state of dissimilarity in terms of views, suttas, and external marks or conduct.

"Mūlasaṅgaha" refers to the Council of the Five Hundred (Pañcasatika-saṅgīti). In phrases such as "collected elsewhere," it means that they extracted various suttas from the collection of suttas already compiled in the Dīgha Nikāya and others, and placed them elsewhere. Or it means they took suttas not included in the original compilation and placed them in some other Nikāya, or made them into something else. "The meaning and the text (attha and dhamma)" refers to the meaning of the Pali and the Pali text itself. "In the Vinaya and in the five Nikāyas" refers to the Vinaya Piṭaka and the remaining five Nikāyas.
48:
The teaching starting with "Ānanda, I have taught feelings in two ways figuratively (pariyāyena)" (Majjhima Nikāya, Bahuvedanīya Sutta, etc.) is a discourse taught by way of figurative or indirect method (pariyāya). Indeed, the Blessed One's inclusion of neutral feeling (upekkhā-vedanā) within peaceful and sublime pleasure (sukha) is the figurative method here. The teaching starting with "Monks, there are these three feelings: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neutral feeling" (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Samādhi Sutta, etc.) is a discourse taught by the direct or literal method (nippariyāya). Indeed, because the nature of feeling is threefold, this is the literal method.

The teaching starting with "Pleasant feeling is also impermanent and conditioned" (Dīgha Nikāya, Mahānidāna Sutta, etc.) is a sutta of explicit meaning (nītattha). The teaching starting with "Whatever is felt, all that is suffering" (Saṃyutta Nikāya, Kaḷāra Sutta, etc.) is a sutta whose meaning is to be inferred (neyyattha). (This is because pleasant and neutral feelings are 'suffering' only in the sense of suffering due to change, vipariṇāma-dukkha.)

In the teaching starting with "Monks, in three respects the people of Jambudīpa surpass the people of Uttarakuru and the Tāvatiṃsa devas" (Aṅguttara Nikāya, Tiṭhāna Sutta, etc.), the Blessed One spoke with reference to another kind of holy life (brahmacariya-vāsa, i.e., monkhood), but the [non-Dhamma speakers] took it and established a different meaning. They also took the sutta starting with "There is no living of the holy life among the devas" and, though it was spoken with reference to one meaning, they established it as having another meaning; thus should the meaning be understood here. By the shadow of the words (literal phrasing) such as "A certain person practices for his own benefit," they destroyed many subtle meanings such as emptiness (suññata/anatta).

"Vinayagambhīra" (profound Vinaya) means discarding a profound portion of the Vinaya (such as the Mahāpadesa or Parivāra). Or it means discarding a sutta that is profound because it can dispel defilements. "Patirūpa" (counterfeit) refers to a sutta that conforms to one's own desires, or a non-sutta that resembles a sutta. Some discarded only the Aṭṭhakathā-kaṇḍa (of the Dhammasaṅgaṇī), while others discarded the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Therefore, it is said (in the Dīpavaṃsa), "Discarding the six books of the Abhidhamma." Although the Kathāvatthu is subject to dispute (vivāda), the other six undisputed books of the Abhidhamma should be recited. To show that those six books no longer existed in the mouths of the non-Dhamma speakers, it is said "six books." Or, it is said "six books" by virtue of the six Abhidhamma treatises that were well-known even before the Third Council.

"Other" refers to other Abhidhamma treatises and so on. "Name" (nāma) refers to the names of Nikāyas that are not associated with the Buddha and others, such as Mañjusirī. "Mark" (liṅga) refers to the specific shape or form created by specific ways of dressing and cloaking. "Requisites" (parikkhāra) refers to items like the carrying-loop (sikkā). "Deportment" (ākappa) should be understood as the specific way of positioning the limbs during standing and so on. "Activity" (karaṇa) refers to specific tasks like sewing robes.

Because they split from the sect or doctrine called Kassapika, they are called "Saṅkantika." Those who split in succession from the Saṅkantika doctrine are the "Suttavāda" individuals. "Bhinnavāda" (schismatic doctrine) is so called because there are divergent doctrines within this [Theravāda context]. When counted together with that [original Theravāda], they become the eighteen doctrines.
49:
The meaning is that together with the undivided Theravāda, there are eighteen doctrines. Alternatively, "bhinnavādena" means there are eighteen by way of divergent views; all those together make eighteen. In the term "Theravādānamuttamo," the word "Thera" is an uninflected designation. That which belongs to the Elders (Theras) such as the Venerable Mahākassapa is "Thera." What is that? It is the doctrine (vāda). The meaning here is that the doctrine of the Elders is the best among doctrines.

With reference to doctrines that have already arisen, it was said: "the crushing of the doctrines of others (parappavāda-mathana)." Because it has the characteristic of preventing doctrines that will arise in the future, it is called "a sign for the future (āyatilakkhaṇa)."

## The Explanation of the Narrative (Nidānakathā) is finished.

## 1. Suddhasaccikaṭṭho
## 1. Anulomapaccayannīkavaṇṇanā
Things like pieces of brick that are seen in the form of gems due to magic are called 'māyā' (illusion). Objects such as magical creations and mirages, which are perceived by the mind in the form of unreal gems or water, are not 'saccikaṭṭha' (real in the true sense) because they possess an unreal nature of being known. To show that a sense such as form or feeling, which is not like those magical creations or mirages but exists truly, is called 'saccikaṭṭha', the Buddha said: 'Māyā ... bhūtattho' (Illusion ... the real sense). A sense perceived through hearsay and so on may be as heard or may be otherwise. Therefore, such a known sense is not 'paramattha' (ultimate reality); only the sense personally realized by oneself is 'paramattha'. To show this, he said: 'Anussavā ... uttamattho' (Hearsay ... the highest sense).

In the word 'chalavādassa', it means the speech that expresses a sense common to the dhammas such as form, which are stated as 'exists' (atthi) by the commonality of the word 'exists'. However, because of the statement 'That person admits ... saccikaṭṭha', it cannot be called 'chalavādassa' (deceptive speech). This is because the view is not 'chala' (deception). 'Okāsaṃ adadamāno' means desiring to cut off the basis [of the argument]. The meaning is: if a person could be obtained by way of 'saccikaṭṭha' (real sense), they should be obtainable like form and so on; since they are not so obtainable, your doctrine cannot stand—thus he refutes it. By the phrase 'taṃ sandhāya', he shows that he refers to the various dhammas mentioned in the Pali passages such as 'rūpañca upalabbhati' (and form is obtained), which are shown by way of being 'sappaccaya' (conditioned) and so on, as stated in 'yo saccikaṭṭho'.

After saying 'tena saccikaṭṭhaparamatthena', the intention of the commentator in saying 'tenākārena' is that a nature obtained by way of the mode of 'saccikaṭṭhaparamattha' is said to be obtained by 'saccikaṭṭhaparamattha'. If it were otherwise (if the mode and the possessor of the mode were different), instead of 'tato', it should have been said 'by that mode of that dhamma'. What is the difference between this second question and the first question? In the first question, it is meant: just as the fifty-seven various dhammas are obtainable by their true individual nature (sabhāva), is the person also obtainable? In this second question, however, it asks: those various dhammas which are obtainable by their true individual nature, are they obtainable by the mode of changeability (ruppana) or being conditioned (sappaccaya) and so on? By that mode...
51:
...is the person also obtained? This is the difference. Just as feeling, which is obtained by its true individual nature like form, is not obtained by the mode of changeability (ruppana), so too the person, who is obtained by true individual nature like the fifty-seven various dhammas, is not obtained by the modes of changeability or being conditioned and so on—this could be argued by the opponent (paravādī), and thus this point would not be open to challenge. Since the opponent's rejection would be appropriate, censure (niggaha) should not be applied. However, because no other real sense (saccikaṭṭha) exists apart from the fifty-seven various dhammas, the challenge is made only by way of the modes of those fifty-seven dhammas. By that very rejection, the fault that leads to censure is shown. The groups of admission and rejection are distinguished as the side of admission, the side of rejection, the affirmative side (anuloma), the negative side (patiloma), the first method, and the second method, due to commonality (sāmaṇya) and specificity (visesa). This should be understood as the difference between these methods.

The proponent (sakavādī), saying 'Tena vata re vattabbe', should be understood as saying 'because it leads to censure' with the intention that the opponent incurs a fault by not saying what ought to be said. It has been said: 'Thus, because the four applications (pāpanā) and impositions (ropanā) are stated by way of censure and the affirmative and negative, it is called the Fivefold Affirmative (anulomapañcaka) starting with "upalabbhati".' However, by way of the affirmative and negative, there should be seven (sattaka) including the two placements (thapanā). Otherwise, the reason for excluding those two placements should be stated. With the intention of saying later: 'A placement (thapanā) is merely the setting up of the opponent's side to show "this is your fault"; it is not a part that can clearly demonstrate censure (niggaha) or rebuttal (paṭikamma),' the two placements are excluded here as well. Just as the fourfold rebuttal (paṭikammacatukka) will be mentioned there instead of the fivefold rebuttal, here too the fourfold censure (niggahacatukka) should be mentioned. However, in a pure censure (suddhikaniggaha) where rebuttal is not mixed, since censure is primary, it should be understood that censure alone is mentioned separately as a summary. In the view of the teachers who say 'Because it is not a true censure, rebuttal is not mentioned separately there,' in the second opening of the discourse (vādamukha), it would result in the fourfold censure and the fivefold rebuttal.

The 'saccikaṭṭha' intended by oneself refers to conventional truth (sammutisacca). For it will be said: 'Referring to pure conventional truth or conventional truth mixed with ultimate reality, the opponent asks again: "yo saccikaṭṭho".' In that case, if the 'saccikaṭṭha' intended by the opponent is conventional truth, then the opponent, who has the same view as the proponent saying 'the person is obtained by way of conventional truth,' should not be refuted. This discussion on the person (puggalakathā) would not even need to be started. Otherwise, the proponent also...
52:
The meaning is this: the opponent (*paravādī*), intending the *saccikaṭṭha* which is conventional truth (*sammuti-sacca*) as desired by him, says "There is that which is *saccikaṭṭha*," and so on. The fault might arise that the proponent (*sakavādī*) also desires only conventional truth as *saccikaṭṭha*. If both he and the proponent desire both conventional truth and ultimate truth (*paramattha-sacca*) as *saccikaṭṭha*, then it should not be said again, "He says this by combining conventional truth and ultimate truth."

If both truths are *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*, the proponent who desires the apprehension of the person by a part of *saccikaṭṭha* (i.e., conventional truth) should not conduct an inquiry such as "Is the person apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact?" nor is an inquiry by a part of *saccikaṭṭha* appropriate. For it is like not being appropriate to inquire whether feeling (*vedanā*), which is apprehended by the mode of being felt (*vedayita*), is apprehended by the mode of being deformed (*ruppana*). The opponent also does not desire the person as having the nature of being deformed, etc., but rather desires the person only as *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha*. If there exists a *saccikaṭṭha* called conventional truth other than ultimate truth, the ultimate truth-ness of that person who is conventional truth should not be inquired into. In the view of teachers who say that the opponent asks intending that conventional *saccikaṭṭha* by attributing the term *saccikaṭṭha* to a person who is not *saccikaṭṭha*, the status of that conventional *saccikaṭṭha* as the *saccikaṭṭha* desired by him is not appropriate. Regarding the status of both conventional *saccikaṭṭha* and ultimate *saccikaṭṭha* as *saccikaṭṭha*, the fault is just as previously stated.

The meaning of *saccikaṭṭha* apprehended by the mode of conventional truth might be apprehended by the mode of true nature (*bhūta-sabhāva*), or it might not. If it is apprehended by the mode of true nature, the opponent who admits "The person is also apprehended in the sense of a real and ultimate fact" should not be inquired into. If it is not apprehended by the mode of true nature, the *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha* mode of the person who is conventional truth, being free from that true nature, should not be stated, because it is not established. It will be said later: "Just as form (*rūpa*) and so on exist by way of individual characteristics (*paccatta-lakkhaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmañña-lakkhaṇa*), the person does not exist in this way." Therefore, the intention of the commentator should be sought here.

In the phrase "of the two truths" (*dvinnaṃ saccānaṃ*), since it is not apprehendable by the mode of the combination of the two truths, this non-attainment should be allowed; otherwise, nothing at all should be said. For just as non-attainment by a part which is the ultimate mode is not a reason for allowance, so also attainment by a part which is the conventional mode is not a reason for rejection; the intention of the commentator should be sought here as well. In the phrase "the mere generality of the word 'is not apprehended'" (*nupalabbhatīti vacanasāmaññamattaṃ*), it means that based on this sophistry (*chala-vāda*), this very word "is it not apprehended?" is both allowed and rejected. Just as I should be refuted by the allowance and rejection of this very word "is apprehended," so also you should be refuted by the allowance and rejection of this very word "is not apprehended." Thus, although it is similar to a statement that should be a ground for refutation (*nigga-haṭṭhāna*), treating a statement that should not be a ground for refutation as one is what constitutes sophistry (*chala-vāda*) here. Therefore, the mere general word "is not apprehended" is called "sophistry" because it is the cause of sophistry. And the mere general word...
53:
It also means "based on sophistry (*chala-vāda*)." It should be examined whether the proposition (*thapanā*) of another's view does not make the meaning of refutation (*niggaha*) and rejoinder (*paṭikamma*) clear. For without setting up a position, it is not possible to charge that admitting the former and denying the latter, or admitting the former while denying the latter, is wrong.

With the intention that the terms *tava* and *paṭijānantaṃ* are usages of the genitive and accusative cases in the sense of the nominative, it was said: "you yourself admitting."

4-5. Because the refutation is brought forward by the four applications of fault (*pāpanāropanā*), by the words "We are well-refuted, if..." etc., it means: "The refutation made by you against me is false, like the refutation made by me against you." Thus, in the fivefold forward sequence (*anuloma-pañcaka*), because the bad state of the refutation made by the four applications of fault is brought forward in that manner along with the refutation made by oneself, or because it has arrived at the state of non-refutation, this is how the meaning should be understood. In this very way, the fourfold conclusion (*nigamana-catukka*) should be understood as the concluding words of the state of non-refutation: "If so, the refutation you make... if... this is false for you."

## The Explanation of the Forward-Negative Sequence is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Negative-Forward Sequence

7-10. After saying "The opponent's admission is based on his own view," it was said again, "The opponent's rejection is because the person does not exist in the ultimate sense." In that statement, if this rejection was made by his own view, then the view "The person is apprehended by another *saccikaṭṭha-paramattha* in the ultimate sense" would be the view of that opponent. In that case, the proponent (*sakavādī*) who accepts that the person exists by way of conventional truth should not refute this opponent. If he hides his own view and rejects by way of another's view, he should not be refuted because it is not contradictory to the previous proposition. For no fault occurs to one who speaks of both his own and another's view. However, the intention here might be that one who admits by his own view and rejects by another's view should be refuted because he has abandoned his own view and taken up another's view.

## The Explanation of the Negative-Forward Sequence is finished.

## 2. Okāsasaccikaṭṭha (The Point on Location in the Real Sense)
## 1. Anulomapaccayānīkavaṇṇanā (Commentary on the Affirmative-Negative)
With the intention of showing that 'sabbattha' (everywhere) means 'in the whole body', it is said 'referring to the body'. In that condensed Pali text, if it is said 'not found in all places' referring to the body, it would follow that 'it is found outside the body'. Therefore, the rejection in the negative is the intention of the Sakavādin. By this statement, the intended meaning is that the person (puggala) is not found by any nature (sabhāva) whatsoever. For there is no location (okāsa) for the finding of a person who is found by any nature, which is free from the body or from anything other than that body.

## 3. Kālasaccikaṭṭha (The Point on Time in the Real Sense)
## 1. Anulomapaccayānīkavaṇṇanā
'Also the times of past and future births' means that it refers to the finding of that very person, who is found in the middle birth-time, in the times of past and future births. The remaining explanation is just the same as what was said in the first method. Among these three, it is just the same as what was said in the first method of 'sabbattha'. What is that similarity? It is the condensed nature of the Pali text. Here too, in this Kālasaccikaṭṭha, if it is said 'not found at all times', it would follow that 'it is found at some time'; therefore, it should be applied that the rejection in the negative is the rejection of the Sakavādin.

## 1. Anulomapaccayānīkavaṇṇanā

## 5. Explanation of the Comparison of the Pure

17-27. "Comparison of the Real and Ultimate Fact with form (rūpa) etc." means the comparison of the person, who is a real and ultimate fact (saccikaṭṭha), with form etc., or the comparison of the person with form etc., in the sense of a real and ultimate fact. In the sentence "Puggalo rūpañca," since the word "ca" has the sense of conjunction (samuccaya), the meaning stated by way of illustration as "like form" should be examined. The doctrine (samaya) is that the person should not be said to be either different or not different from form etc. There is the Sutta Pali: "The soul is one thing, the body is another—this has not been declared (abyākata) by the Blessed One," etc. Intending this meaning—that if one were to admit it, it would lead to a contradiction with both that doctrine and the Sutta—it is said: "Seeing the contradiction with the doctrine and the Sutta."

"Dhammato" means according to the Pali text. The commentators who say, "The fourfold rebuttal (paṭikamma-catukka) etc., are summarized. The opponent (paravādin)... etc... are shown," will see the Pali "Ājānāhi niggahaṃ" (Recognize the refutation) in this Pali "Puggalo nupalabbhati... etc... ājānāhi."
56:
In this context of "Paṭikamma," the reading "Ājānāhi niggahaṃ" will be found. "Aññattaṃ paṭijānāpanatthaṃ" means for the purpose of urging one to admit to being "other," in the sense: "Just as I ought to say it is other, so too should you say it." "Sammuti-paramatthānaṃ ekatta-nānatta-pañhassa thapanīyattā" means because the question of the identity or difference between the conventional (sammuti) and the ultimate (paramattha) is to be set aside (thapanīya/abyākata).

If it should be rejected because it is to be set aside, then the opponent (paravādin) also made the rejection based on their own view because it is to be set aside; thus, that opponent should also not be refuted. However, the opponent takes some nature (sabhāva) to be a "person" and desires that question to be set aside. If a nature exists, setting it aside is not appropriate; therefore, the opponent should be refuted. But the person who is a conventional designation is not any ultimate nature. For that very reason, the proponent (sakavādin) who says that the question of its identity or difference is to be set aside should not be refuted. Therefore, the intention here is that it is appropriate that the proponent made the rejection.

## The Explanation of the Comparison of the Pure is finished.

## 6. Explanation of the Comparison by Simile

28-36. This statement "Upaladdhi-sāmaññena aññatta-pucchā ca" (And the question of difference through commonality of perception) should also be examined. The similarity in the possibility of obtaining (upalabbhanīya) both form and feeling is not appropriate as a reason for being "other." Indeed, it should be examined that only the possibility of obtaining by way of one's own distinct nature as a real and ultimate fact (saccikaṭṭha-paramattha) is appropriate as a reason for being "other." "Ekavīsādhikāni" is an old reading, but it should be recited and read only as "Vīsādhikāni."

37-45. ## 7. Explanation of the Comparison of the Fourfold Method

46-52. An opponent who does not wish for the person to be different from even a single phenomenon among the fifty-seven types of phenomena should not be questioned or examined by way of each individual phenomenon such as form (rūpa). The reason is that, to prevent the opportunity for this opponent—who does not wish for the person to be different from the collective whole of phenomena like form and feeling, but rejects non-difference from a part such as form—to say that they do not deserve refutation, the [Commentator] said "And this inquiry" (ayañca anuyogo), etc. "Sakalā" (the whole) means intending the entirety in this way: "Are the fifty-seven types of phenomena the person?" or "Is the ultimate truth the person?" Having thus considered the entire ultimate reality, because the characteristic of inquiry and examination is established by way of the sequence of the Pāḷi text, and because there is no person in the sense of ultimate reality (saccikaṭṭha) other than the entire ultimate reality, it is meant that it is appropriate to impose a refutation on the opponent who rejects the question "Is form the person?" on the grounds that a person who is an ultimate reality cannot be other than that entire ultimate reality.

"Sabhāgavinibbhogato" means by way of having a nature such as feeling, etc., which is different from the nature of form. By the words "all phenomena" (sabbadhammā), it refers to all the remaining fifty-six phenomena, excluding form. ## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of Falling Away in Terms of Argumentative Logic

"Bhikkhus, these two things lead to the falling away of a trainee bhikkhu" (A. Ni. 2.185). In the phrase "Having been future or present, it is" (Anāgataṃ vā paccuppannaṃ vā hutvā hoti), it should be noted that when a future phenomenon becomes future and then becomes present, it is said to be "having been future, it is present." (Kiṃ te tampi hutvā hoti) means: because of the non-departure of that state of "having been, it is," it is a question about the non-cessation or continuity of the state of "having been, it is." "Because there is no further 'having been' for what has already been" (Hutvā bhūtassa puna hutvā abhāvato) means: because a phenomenon that was future and has become present does not become future and present again.

Since that phenomenon which was future and became present is reckoned as "having been, it is," therefore, the teacher's intention is that he admits the second expression "having been, it is" is also appropriate. To one who speaks of the non-cessation of the state of "having been, it is" regarding ultimate phenomena (dhamma), the non-cessation of the state of "not having been, it is not" regarding non-ultimate things like a rabbit's horn (sasa-visāṇa) would follow; with this intention, it says "Atha naṃ," etc.

## 10. Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional Expression
In the Discourse on Conventional Expression (Vohārakathā), regarding the phrase "Or are the ear and so on [supramundane]?", there is no reason why, among objects (visaya) and subjects/possessors of objects (visayī) which are exclusively mundane, only the object should have a supramundane nature while the subjects do not. Just as the supramundane nature of the subjects is not established, so too the supramundane nature of the sound-base (saddāyatana), which is an object, is not established. Among those (objects and subjects), just as that sound-base, whose supramundane nature is not established, reaches a supramundane state (according to your view), so too the ear and so on reach a supramundane state. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: "Are those ear-faculties and so on also supramundane?"

The meaning "If it were to strike against the supramundane (ear), it would be a supramundane expression" should not be accepted. This is because, even if it is imagined that it strikes against the supramundane, the supramundane nature of the sound-base does not exist; thus, this meaning should not be taken. Although the author cites "by mundane knowledge" (lokiyena ñāṇena), the Pali text actually has "by consciousness" (viññāṇena). That consciousness is understood as ear-consciousness (sotaviññāṇa) because it is connected with the ear-sensitivity (sotapasāda). "Non-exclusivity" (anekantatā) means that the reason "it is mundane because it is known by mundane knowledge" would lead to non-exclusivity (indeterminacy) because it can occur in both the mundane and the supramundane.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Conventional Expression is finished.

## 11. Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation
"Does not desire two truths of suffering" means that the opponent does not desire those two truths of suffering which ought to have two types of cessation (namely, cessation not through deliberation and cessation through deliberation). By the Pali "not ceased through deliberation by supramundane knowledge" and so on, those formations (saṅkhāra) that cease without deliberation and do not occur are shown as "ceased without deliberation" (appaṭisaṅkhāniruddha). It does not mean the destruction after arising (momentary cessation). By showing it thus, it amounts to showing that cessation not through deliberation (appaṭisaṅkhā-nirodha) is the cessation consisting in non-occurrence (asamudācaraṇa-nirodha).

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Cessation is finished.

## 3. The Third Chapter
## 1. Explanation of the Discourse on Powers
The statement that the knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties (indriyaparopariyatta-ñāṇa) is unique (to the Buddha) means that although disciples (sāvaka) know the possible and the impossible (ṭhānāṭhāna) and so on in brief by way of summary, such as "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that a person endowed with right view should regard any formation as permanent," they do not know the knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties even in brief, such as "He knows the disposition, he knows the underlying tendency." Therefore, it is called "unique" (asādhāraṇa).

The statement by the Elder Anuruddha, "I know the proficiency of the faculties of beings as it really is," was said with reference only to knowing the sharpness or dullness of the faculties such as faith (saddhā) and so on. It should be understood in this context that it does not refer to the Power of the Tathāgata (Tathāgatabala) which is the knowledge of the proficiency of the faculties mentioned above. It is said, "He claims [to know] by way of knowing the possible and impossible and so on in brief." If one claims thus, it would also mean claiming that "the Power of the Tathāgata is common to the disciples" in the same way. If that were so, how should this opponent be questioned?

The rejection regarding the remaining (knowledges) means that the proponent (Sakavādin) rejects them with reference to the part that is common, among the common and unique aspects of the knowledge of the possible and impossible and so on.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on Powers is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Discourse on 'Noble'
For the person who makes a claim with reference to formations (saṅkhāra), it should be investigated how the meeting of two touches (phassa) occurs according to the method mentioned above. A being is called a "fixation" (paṇidhi) because of being established by being superimposed through false imagination. That fixation should not be established by superimposing it even on a single aggregate. Therefore, the state of being empty of that fixation (being) which is established by superimposing it even on a single aggregate is stated.

## The Explanation of the Discourse on 'Noble' is finished.

## 4. Vimuccamānakathā-vaṇṇanā

## 7. Exposition of the Dibba-cakkhu-kathā
Upatthaddha (supported) means the infusion of power through the state (of the fourth jhāna) which is the cause for making it distinct through the power of repeated occurrence and the ability to take an object. Taṃ-mattam-eva means that the fleshly eye (maṃsa-cakkhu) as it was before, prior to the infusion of power, is not supported by the Dhamma. Anāpāthagata refers to things that have not come into the range of vision, which is the place to be grasped by the fleshly eye (i.e., things hidden by mountains, walls, etc.). Here, the intention is to show the similarity of the object and the dissimilarity of the power and range (ānu-bhāva-gocara). In taking the object as "What is the object of the fleshly eye?", it is not to show the distinction of the object, but rather to show such a visible object (rūpārammaṇa) in which there are special powers and ranges, or to show the distinction of the power and range even in the same object.

He does not wish that the fleshly eye itself is the divine eye means he does not wish that the fleshly eye as it was before is the divine eye at the time it is supported by the Dhamma. Saying "The arising of the fleshly eye is the path (magga)" is said only to show that the fleshly eye is a cause, and not to establish the state of being unclung-to (anupādinnatā) by that statement. Rūpāvacarikānaṃ means the great elements (mahābhūta) that have arisen due to the cause of fine-material sphere absorption (rūpāvacara-jhāna) are called "belonging to the fine-material sphere"; this is what that opponent intends. This same method applies to the word arūpāvacarikānaṃ. "He rejects it because there is no fine-material sphere mind at the moment of the formless sphere" means he rejects it because at that very moment, being of the fine-material sphere, it cannot be of the formless sphere.

Even if he does not wish for the divine eye supported by wisdom to be the eye of wisdom (paññā-cakkhu), the meaning is that if someone, because of the support of the Dhamma, speaks of it as being a different kind of eye, then in his doctrine, there would be three eyes: the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the eye of wisdom.

## Exposition of the Dibba-cakkhu-kathā is finished.

## 4. Commentary on Dānakathā

"To urge by the power of the gift-object (deyyadhamma)" means to urge with the thought: if only the mental factor (intention/cetanā) is the gift (dāna), then by the meaning "it is called dāna because it is given," wouldn't the nature of dāna belong only to the mental factor of intention?

It should be understood that the word "aniṭṭhaphalā" (undesirable result) and so on is said for the purpose of showing the nature of dāna in non-mental things (such as food, etc.), and not for the purpose of showing the manifestation of the giving of results. By the word "aniṭṭhaphalā" and so on, it is as if the giving of results by non-mental things is stated, but it is not stating the nature of dāna; this word was said for the purpose of preventing that giving of results. Having done so, immediately after that, it was said, "Non-mental things such as food do not give a resultant (vipāka) in the future." "For the purpose of always determining the state of desirable results (iṭṭhaphalā)" means that there is no undesirable result of dāna in any way like the gift-object, but it is for the purpose of determining that it is certainly only a desirable result.

"Itarena" means by the method "it is called dāna because it is given." "Na pana ekenatthena" means that to refute the Theravāda (Sakavādī) view that "only the gift-object is dāna," the sutta evidence such as "faith, shame" is suitable in the opponent's view (Paravādī); the sutta such as "here someone gives food" is also the same. To refute the opponent's view that "only the mental factor is dāna" and to establish the view that "the mental factor is dāna," the sutta such as "faith, shame" is suitable in the Theravāda view. The sutta such as "here someone gives food" is suitable for establishing that "the gift-object is dāna." It should be noted that "na pana ekenatthena" was said with reference to this difference between the purpose of refutation and the purpose of establishment. Among those two views, just as in the opponent's view, for the sake of sutta evidence, the meaning "only the mental factor" should be noted in the question "it should not be said that the mental factor is dāna," likewise, in the question "it should not be said that the gift-object is dāna," the meaning "only the gift-object" should be noted. In the context of "the gift-object has a desirable result," here, by the text "iṭṭhaphalābhāvamatāmeva paṭikkhittaṁ," only the absence of desirable results is refuted...

"Bhavitabbaṃ" (it should be) should be noted. Alternatively, it should be said, "It is rejected seeing only the absence of the desired result." In the phrase "for the sake of freeing from being mixed in nature," it means for the sake of freeing from the state of giving (dāna), both in the sense of the mental factor of volition (cetanā) being what should be given, and in the sense of the gift (deyyadhamma) having the desired result.

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion on Merit Consisting in Use (Paribhogamaya-puñña-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

There is a view that there is merit dissociated from the mind (citta-vippayutta) which arises from the recipient's use [of a gift]. Those opponents (paravādī), referring to that merit dissociated from the mind consisting in use, say, "Merit consisting in the recipient's use increases."

"Tassāpi vasena" means also by the power of the view that there is a combination of those five consciousnesses (the opponent admits this). It is said that they admit it, thinking that there should be a combination of both types of merit arising from the recipient's use, like the five consciousnesses. However, it means they admit it referring only to the combination of the five consciousnesses, contact (phassa), and so on.

By the words "aparibhuttepi," the text shows the statement such as "the recipient, after receiving, does not use it but throws it away." This view of the opponent, that "merit consisting in the recipient's use increases" because there is merit even when the gift is not used, is inferior. When that opponent's view is inferior, the proponent's (sakavādī) view is strong. It means that the state of merit of only the volition of giving (cāga-cetanā) is established in this aforementioned way. Because the state of merit belongs only to the volition of giving even when the gift is not used, it is said, "Only the proponent's view is strong."

## The Commentary on the Discussion on Merit Consisting in Use is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion on "Is the Earth a Result of Kamma?" (Pathavī-kamma-vipāko-ti-kathā-vaṇṇanā)

By the statement that contact (phassa) is of various kinds such as that to be experienced as pleasant (sukha-vedanīya), etc., all results of kamma (kamma-vipāka) are shown through contact. Then, to show the association with states such as feeling (vedanā) and perception (saññā) which are excluded from itself (contact), it is said, "That contact and those perceptions, etc." The phrase "it exists for them" is said referring to the co-nascent states such as eye-consciousness (cakkhu-viññāṇa) together with advertence (āvajjana). Among those (results), whatever desired result there is, "longing for that result" means they perform kamma by longing only for the desired result; thus it shows the longing which is a decisive support (upanissaya) for kamma. Alternatively, craving (taṇhā) which has present feeling as its condition causes suffering to arise through the power of producing grasping (upādāna), etc. "Root craving" (mūla-taṇhā) refers either to the craving in a previous life which is the decisive support for the kamma that produces the present round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa), or to the craving which is the companion of kamma and the decisive support for the result.

To show the suitability in the challenge even by the power of their own view, he said, "Also by the view of those," and so on.

By the words "by the power of obtaining," he shows that when there is kamma, there is the obtaining of the earth, etc.; thus kamma is said to be "conducive to that (result)."

## The Commentary on the Discussion on "Is the Earth a Result of Kamma?" is finished.

Some teachers say, "The state of having an impure complexion is indeed old age." That statement is just the same as the statement showing the ugliness of only the material form (rūpa), such as "unwholesome kamma is of the kamma-produced (material form)..."

## 9. Explanation of the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena

"And the state of being a proximity condition (anantarapaccayatañceva)" means that ignorance (avijjā) assists formations (saṅkhārā) by way of proximity condition. There is that which is the standing or the cause of standing of ignorance; because of that standing or cause of standing, that proximity force (anantara-satti) arises. The meaning is that the standing or cause of standing, which is called the state of being a proximity condition, arises along with that standing or cause of standing.

In this context, the taking of the proximity condition should be understood as having the purpose of showing a single proximity condition that is devoid of the state of being a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccaya). By showing that one type of condition, all conditions similar to that proximity condition are shown.

"And the state of being a mutuality condition (aññamaññapaccayatañca)" means that ignorance is a condition for formations, and formations are also conditions for ignorance. In that case, because of the standing or cause of standing called the state of ignorance being a condition for formations, the standing or cause of standing called the state of formations being a condition for ignorance arises; and because of that standing or cause of standing of formations, the other standing or cause of standing of ignorance arises. This is the meaning.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Stability of Phenomena is finished.

## 1. Explanation of the Discussion on Restraint and Action

630-632. "Resultant door (vipākadvāra)" refers to the life-continuum mind (bhavaṅga-citta). "Kamma door (kammadvāra)" refers to wholesome and unwholesome minds.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Restraint and Action is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Discussion on Kamma

633-635. "Rejection with reference to the indeterminate (abyākataṃ sandhāya paṭikkhepo)" means it is said that the rejection is made by way of the characteristic of one's own doctrine (sakavāda). Thinking that if the indeterminate (abyākata) volition is shown in its true nature, then the volition that yields results (wholesome and unwholesome) is also already shown, it was said: "In order to show the volition that yields results and the volition that does not yield results in their true nature."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on Kamma is finished.

## 3. Explanation of the Discussion on "Sound is a Resultant"

636-637. By the words "Whether mental phenomena born of kamma (kammasamuṭṭhānā arūpadhammā vā)," etc., it is shown that even in the case of physical phenomena such as the eye which are born of kamma, the term "resultant" (vipāka) is not used; how much less, then, could there be any reason to call sound "resultant," which is not even born of kamma?

## The Explanation of the Discussion on "Sound is a Resultant" is finished.
98:
## 4. Explanation of the Discussion on the Six Sense Bases

638-640. In the phrase "Therefore, it is a resultant," it means that the view of certain people is that "all six sense bases are resultants," without specifying any particular sense base.

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Six Sense Bases is finished.

## 5. Explanation of the Discussion on the Seven-times-at-most [Person]

641-645. "Fixed as a seven-times-at-most person (sattakkhattuparama-tāniyato)" means one who is certain in the state of being a seven-times-at-most person. "This distinction" refers to this specific difference. "Do you desire the fixed certainty of that person?" means: do you desire a fixed certainty in another state of being a seven-times-at-most person by way of the state of one not subject to downfall (avinipāta-dhammatā) and the attainment of the fruition (phala) immediately after one's own path?

"The absence of heinous kamma (ānantariya-kammābhāvaṃ)" means the absence of that heinous kamma by which a person would be called one incapable of penetrating the Dhamma; or it means that the seven-times-at-most stream-enterer (sotāpanna) is not one who possesses heinous kamma. Indeed, if it is asked whether that person will penetrate the Dhamma within the seven lives, some teachers say: "The seven-times-at-most person does not exceed the seventh life, but there is no prohibition against attaining the Dhamma within those seven lives."

Other teachers, however, say: "For a person whom the Blessed One has predicted by the power of His knowledge, there is no such thing as penetration of the Dhamma within the seven lives; nevertheless, because there is no fixed certainty of lives, he is called 'capable' (bhabba). For example, just as wholesome super-knowledge volitions (abhiññā-cetanā) are called 'phenomena of the nature of result' (vipākadhamma-dhammā) because they have the capacity to give results when the cause is present, even if they do not give results at times; likewise, the seven-times-at-most person exists because of the weakness of the faculties (indriya), not because of the existence of a fixed certainty of lives (bhava-niyāma), nor because of the Blessed One's prediction. Furthermore, since the weakness of faculties is not a phenomenon that causes the state of being incapable (abhabba) of attaining the Dhamma within the seven lives, that person cannot be called 'incapable' (abhabba). The state of being incapable is denied here because of the absence of phenomena that cause such incapacity, but it does not mean the state of being capable (bhabba) of penetrating the Dhamma within the seven lives. If the seven-times-at-most person were to penetrate the Dhamma within the seven lives, he would become a 'Kolankola' person." However, without making a specific distinction, it is appropriate to call him "capable (bhabba)" due to his capable nature. In the phrase "There is no phenomenon that fixes the lives," the words "having seen" are omitted, or it should be connected forward as "does not predict."

## The Explanation of the Discussion on the Seven-times-at-most [Person] is finished.

## The Explanation of the Twelfth Chapter is finished.

## 13. Terasamavagga

## 1. Kappaṭṭhakathāvaṇṇanā

654-657. In the Kappaṭṭhakathā, "below" refers to the Iddhibalakathā (referring to the intended meaning).

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Kappaṭṭhakathā.

## 3. Anantarāpayuttakathāvaṇṇanā

660-662. In the Anantarāpayuttakathā, because this person (the instigator) has instigated an immediate offense (ānantariya-kamma), they are called "anantarāpayutta". It should be understood that the meaning is stated in the Commentary by metaphorically applying the word "anantarā" to the immediate offense. The Pali text is also seen as "anantarapayutto".

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Anantarāpayuttakathā.

## 4. Niyatassaniyāmakathāvaṇṇanā

663-664. In this passage, "The remaining states belonging to the three planes are called undetermined (aniyata)", the phrase "states belonging to the three planes" is said with reference to those states that have not yet reached the assurance (niyāma) [of rightness or wrongness]. Indeed, with reference to those very persons, it is said, "Even though endowed with those states, they are still undetermined." Thus, taking only this conventional usage, those who hold the view, "The destined Bodhisatta, who is in his final existence (pacchimabhavika), is capable of penetrating the Dhamma and entering [the assurance]," interpret the meaning as "He enters the assurance." In this way, the mere existence of the designation "destined" (niyata) is stated as the reason for the word "niyato", and the capability to penetrate the Dhamma is stated as the reason for the words "niyāmaṃ okkamati". However, it is more appropriate to say that the capability (bhabbatā) itself is the reason for both. The phrase "by another reason" means that if a destined person were to enter the assurance—if one destined for wrongness (micchattaniyata) were to enter the assurance of rightness (sammattaniyāma), or one destined for rightness were to enter the assurance of wrongness—it is stated to show that such a thing does not exist.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Niyatassaniyāmakathā.

## 8. Asātarāgakathāvaṇṇanā
In the Asātarāgakathā, greed that arises in the form "Oh, may this very thing be mine!" (aho vata me etadeva bhaveyya) is intended here as "lust" (rāga), and it shows that it is not intended in any other way. The word "Sutte pana" is connected with the word "adhippāyo".

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Asātarāgakathā.

## 9. Dhammataṇhāabyākatātikathāvaṇṇanā
676-680. Because it is called "craving for states" (dhamma-taṇhā), taking the craving that arises for wholesome states or for all supramundane states as "craving for states", it shows the view that because that state is craving, it is not wholesome, and because it arises regarding states (Dhamma), it is not unwholesome, thus it is "indeterminate" (abyākata). Since the six types of craving have already been shown in summary by way of the three groups, the meaning is that craving for states is also not indeterminate because it is of the nature of craving for sensual pleasures (kāma-taṇhā), and so on.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Dhammataṇhāabyākatātikathā.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Thirteenth Chapter.

## 14. Cuddasamavagga

## 1. Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathāvaṇṇanā
686-690. The word "taṃ" should be seen as connected separately to "wholesome" and "unwholesome". Alternatively, it should be seen as an ellipsis for "taṃ ubhayaṃ" (both of them). "Paṭisandahati" means it connects, or it means it causes to arise immediately after.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Kusalākusalapaṭisandahanakathā.
101:
## 2. Saḷāyatanuppattikathāvaṇṇanā
691-692. Some theorists (such as the Kapila teachers) say, "In the sprout, the mere seed of trees and so on, which are endowed with branches, twigs, etc., becomes manifest." Desiring to show their view as an illustration, he said "sampannasākhāviṭapānaṃ", and so on.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Saḷāyatanuppattikathā.

## 3. Anantarapaccayakathāvaṇṇanā
693-697. In the passage, "Dependent on the eye and forms, ear-consciousness arises," when it is said that one admits this by the power of one's own view, even though one notices the arising of ear-consciousness immediately after eye-consciousness, that person does not intend ear-consciousness that takes a form as its object at the eye-sensitivity (cakkhu-pasāda); rather, they intend only the taking of a sound as its object at the ear-sensitivity (sota-pasāda). Therefore, because it occurs by the power of the view of obtaining [the result] in proximity, it is appropriate to say "he admits".

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Anantarapaccayakathā.

## 4. Ariyarūpakathāvaṇṇanā
698-699. The opponent (paravādī), who desires that the path-factors such as right speech are both form (rūpa) and the path (magga), also says "noble form" (ariyarūpa).

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Ariyarūpakathā.

## 5. Aññoanusayotikathāvaṇṇanā
700-701. Between the former reading, "sarāgo" etc., meaning it should be called "with lust" because lust has not yet been abandoned at that time, and the latter reading, "sānusayo" etc., meaning it should be called "with underlying tendency" because the underlying tendency has not yet been abandoned at that time, the latter reading is appropriate. This is because that reading is consistent with the statement that it cannot be proven because the underlying tendency (anusaya) and the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) are not different from each other.

## Conclusion of the Commentary on the Aññoanusayotikathā.

## 6. Pariyuṭṭhānaṃcittavippayuttantikathāvaṇṇanā
Because defilements such as lust arise even in a person who is contemplating with respect to impermanence and so on, and even when they arise, those such as lust are not associated with insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), therefore, the meaning is that there is a view that the uprising of defilements (pariyuṭṭhāna) is dissociated from the mind.

## The Commentary on the Discussion that Obsession is Dissociated from Mind is finished.

## 7. Pariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā
703-705. 'Because there are three divisions' means there are three divisions either by way of the objects of defilement (kilesavatthu), the physical basis (vatthu-kāma), and the space of the sensual realm (okāsa); or by way of sensual lust (kāmarāga), sensual thought (kāmavitakka), and the dhammas belonging to the sense sphere (kāmāvacaradhamma). 'By way of kilesakāma' means by way of being the element of sensuality (kāmadhātu) which is the defilement of sensuality. 'Being unable to note the meaning' means the meaning is being unable to note the fact of being asked whether it underlies by way of being associated with the fine-material element (rūpadhātu), or whether it is included in the fine-material element by way of being one of the fine-material dhammas.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Inclusion is finished.

## 8. Abyākatakathāvaṇṇanā
706-708. Wrong view is linked as being called 'undeclared' (abyākata) because it was not spoken of by way of being eternal and so on, as in 'Vaccha, this view that the world is eternal is undeclared (not answered by the Buddha)'. Here, however, wrong view is not taught as 'undeclared'; rather, it is shown that 'this question is to be set aside (ṭhapanīya)'. Therefore, it is quite appropriate that wrong view should not be called 'undeclared' in every respect.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Undeclared is finished.

## 9. Apariyāpannakathāvaṇṇanā
709-710. 'Therefore' means because even though there is equality in the fact that both view (diṭṭhi) and lust (rāga) are suppressed (vikkhamphana) by jhāna, there is a convention of saying 'one free from lust' but no convention of saying 'one free from view'; thus they say the meaning is that view is not included in the mundane (apariyāpanna). Since there is no view in the fine-material realm (rūpabhūmi), it should only be a view included in the sensual element (kāmadhātu). If it were included (pariyāpanna), then...
103:
If view were also to disappear for the jhāna-attainer like sensual lust, one should be able to say "one who has discarded view," but it is not said so; therefore, view is unincluded (apariyāpanna). It should be understood that [the opponent] says that the view not yet discarded by that jhāna-attainer is not a sensual view that causes inclusion in the sensual element like sensual lust.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Unincluded is finished.

## The Commentary on the Fourteenth Chapter is finished.

## 1. Paccayatākathāvaṇṇanā

711-717. Therefore, "the state of being a condition is determined" means that just as a dhamma which is a root-condition (hetu-paccaya) should not become an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya) etc., or a predominance-condition (adhipati-paccaya) etc., only its state as a root-condition is determined.

718-719. "Is not ignorance co-nascent with formations?" Because of this statement, it means only the formation of demerit (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) is taken. In the phrase "by way of co-nascence (sahajāta), mutuality (aññamañña), presence (atthi), non-disappearance (avigata), and association (sampayutta)," the support-condition (nissaya-paccaya) is not mentioned separately because it is already included by taking the presence-condition (atthi-paccaya) out of sequence; this is to be understood because of the specific nature of the kamma-condition and nutriment-condition. It will be said later: "The three graspings are conditions for formations because of ignorance, just as they are conditions because of craving." Therefore, here the conditionality of formations is shown to be just like that of the graspings.

## 9. Tatiyasaññāvedayitakathāvaṇṇanā

In the third discussion of perception and feeling, "referring to the remaining beings" means referring to those five-constituent beings (pañcavokāra-satta) other than the person who has entered the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), for whom the attainment of cessation is possible. "The natural state of the body" means this body is of such a nature; in a body of such a nature, even the touch of a hand can occur, and so on.

733-734. "It would be contrary to the Sutta"—this statement should be made after making the opponent admit it.

## 10. Asaññasattupikakathāvaṇṇanā

In stating the view that "the meditation proceeding by way of revulsion towards perception is the attainment of non-perception," it shows the opponent's view that without taking the fourth jhāna attainment, which is the meditation proceeding by way of revulsion towards perception, as the "attainment of non-perception," that state of being non-percipient is also just the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha-samāpatti). Because in the phrase "one who has entered the attainment of non-perception has non-greed etc.," the fourth jhāna attainment established in one's own school (Sakavāda) is called the "attainment of non-perception."

It is the state of being non-percipient because of entering it by way of revulsion towards perception, not because of the absence of perception—this refers only to the fourth jhāna attainment.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Non-percipient Beings is finished.

## 11. Kammūpacayakathāvaṇṇanā

738-739. In the questions "Is it co-nascent with kamma?", there is a reading in some places: "He rejects it referring to the accumulation of kamma (kammūpacaya), and accepts it referring to what is dissociated from mind (cittavippayutta)."
105:
In another version (manuscript), it says: "He rejects it referring to what is associated with consciousness, and accepts it referring to what is dissociated from consciousness." Both of these should be examined. Therefore, it should be understood that the meaning is that [the Proponent] asks about the oneness because the three—Kamma, Kammūpacaya (accumulation of kamma), and Kammavipāka (result of kamma)—exist at the same moment, and also because of the combination of the three contacts (phassa).

## The Explanation of Kammūpacayakathā is finished.

## 3. Explanation of Sukhanuppadānakathā

747-748. In the Sukhanuppadānakathā, "yaṃ evarūpaṃ" means: there is such happiness that is not one's own property, nor the property of others, nor that person's property; such a thing called happiness is not fit to be given, because one is unable to give another's happiness. 749-753. "Tañcittatāya" means: that person has that very mind as an object; therefore, that person is called "tañcitta" (having that mind). The state of that person is "tañcittatā." It means to raise an objection by that state of tañcittatā. Alternatively, that mind which is the subject and object of cognition is "tañcitta." Its state is "tañcittatā." It means to raise an objection by that tañcittatā, which is the state of being both the subject and object of that very mind.

768-770. In the Rūpaṃ rūpāvacara-arūpāvacaranti-kathā, "heṭṭhā" (below) refers to the Pariyāpannakathā in the fourteenth chapter (Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā 703-705). It is the same method as mentioned starting with "samāpattesiyaṃ."

## 17. The Seventeenth Chapter

## 1. Explanation of the Discourse: An Arahant has Accumulation of Merit

776-779. "Without taking the mind" means: without taking the functional mind (kiriya-citta) which is indeterminate (abyākata), as it was said, "because of the existence of the occurrence of giving etc. with the functional mind" (he establishes his view).

## The Explanation of the Discourse: An Arahant has Accumulation of Merit is finished.

## 2. Explanation of the Discourse: An Arahant has no Untimely Death

"Taking by improper means" means: taking the meaning as "I do not say there is the total exhaustion of kammas that have not yet had the opportunity to ripen." Some teachers say, "Taking the meaning improperly as: I do not say there is the total exhaustion of a person without having experienced the results of kammas."

"Cannot enter for that long" is a rejection by view. It means: it cannot enter for that long (the poison), but it can enter after that kamma is exhausted—this is the rejection by view. Here, because of the statement "he deprives one of life while life still remains, while a remnant of life exists," teachers say that there is no offense of killing (pāṇātipāta) for one who strikes or cuts off the head of one who is dying naturally. Even though the factors—a living being, the perception of a living being, the intent to kill, the effort, and death—are present, since the person did not die because of that effort, there is no offense of killing. It is very difficult to know that such a dying person does not die even a single mind-moment earlier than the natural death.

## The Explanation of the Discourse: An Arahant has no Untimely Death is finished.
107:
## 3. Explanation of Sabbamidaṃ kammatoti-kathā

In the phrase "as a sprout from a seed," just as a sprout cannot arise from something other than a seed, so too the continuous present aggregates cannot arise from anything other than the result of kamma (kammavipāka), not from non-kamma. It means he rejects it referring to this absence. "He asks about the fruit of giving by way of the gift" means: regarding the gift, he gives it with a certain intention (cetanā); he asks about the fruit of that intention of giving, not the fruit of the material gift itself.

## The Explanation of Sabbamidaṃ kammatoti-kathā is finished.

## 4. Explanation of Indriyabaddhakathā

In the phrase "even apart from impermanence," just as in the Pali texts such as "hells are extremely painful," it means it should be called suffering (dukkha) also because it is an object of painful feeling.

## The Explanation of Indriyabaddhakathā is finished.

## 7. Explanation of the Discourse: It should not be said that the Saṅgha purifies the gift

793-794. In the discourse "It should not be said that the Saṅgha purifies the gift," "those Paths and Fruitions cannot purify the gift" means: just as a person can purify by purifying their virtue or by attaining the attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti), the Paths and Fruitions cannot do so. Or it means because they do not receive the gift.

## The Explanation of the Discourse: It should not be said that the Saṅgha purifies the gift is finished.

## 11. Explanation of Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā

800-801. In the Dakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā, to show the meaning of "would be purified," it says "would be of great fruit." In the phrase "only the purity of the donor's mind gives the result," it means that without depending on the recipient, and even without the recipient as a condition, the donor's mind alone brings about the state of intention for a great result; thus it gives the result without depending on the recipient. Another person's...
108:
Regarding the term "doer" (kāraka), why is it said, "If the donor's intention to give were performed by the recipient, it would be appropriate"? In stating the doctrine, is it not said, "The donor gives the gift, the recipient brings about the result (vipāka); thus, one person would be the doer for another"? This is true. However, the meaning is that if the recipient's bringing about of the result were also through the bringing about of the intention to give, then in that case, it would be appropriate to say, "one person is the doer for another."

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Purity of Gifts (Dakkhināvisuddhikathā) is finished.

## The Commentary on the Seventeenth Chapter (Vagga) is finished.

802-803. "Unwisely" (ayoniso) refers to the wrong view such as "referring to the Tusita heaven."

813-816. 109:
## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Intermediate Jhana (Jhānantarikakathā)

817-819. This so-called intermediate jhana (jhānantarika) is not a jhana because it does not have the nature of any of the jhanas such as the first jhana. 826-827. In the phrase "referring to cognition" (paṭizānanaṃ sandhāya), the meaning is that it refers to the cognition by mind-consciousness (manoviññāṇa) taught in the manner of "Having seen a form with the eye, one grasps at its signs" (Dhs. 1352), etc. Therefore, it should be examined: "If this is so, the form reaches the mind-consciousness; how then can cognition by mind-consciousness be called the seeing of form?"

## 19. The Nineteenth Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of Defilements (Kilesapajahanakathā)

828-831. The opponent objects that there is no abandoning of defilements, saying that only unarisen defilements are said to be abandoned because they do not arise. He shows that it should not be said that "one abandons past defilements," etc., by stating that those defilements have neither arisen and passed away, nor will they arise, nor are they presently arisen.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Abandoning of Defilements is finished.
110:
## 2. Commentary on the Discussion of Emptiness (Suññatakathā)

By the words "The characteristic of non-self is partial" (anattalakkhaṇaṃ tāva ekaccaṃ), he speaks of the characteristic of non-self of the immaterial aggregates. Regarding the words "by a certain method" (ekena pariyāyena), they (the teachers) say it is by the method of the state of aging and death of the characteristic of non-self. Indeed, the state of non-self (anattatā) is the mode of not being under one's control (avasavattanākāra), which cannot be obtained by wishing for the aggregate of matter, etc., "May it not decay, may it not die." That non-self is, in essence, only aging and death. And since it is said, "Aging and death are included in two aggregates" (Dhātuk. 71), the aging and death of the immaterial aggregates are included in the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha). This is the intention of those teachers.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Emptiness is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Discussion of the Fruits of Recluseship (Sāmaññaphalakathā)

835-836. By the words "and the attainment of the fruit" (phaluppatti ca), he speaks of the nature of attainment.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Fruits of Recluseship is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Discussion of Thusness (Tathatākathā)

841-843. In the phrase "known as the nature of form, etc." (rūpādisabhāvatāsaṅkhātā), the meaning should be understood as the state of being the nature of form and so on. This "thusness" (tathatā) refers only to the nature (bhāva) itself, not to the association with the nature (bhāvayoga).

## The Commentary on the Discussion of Thusness is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome (Kusalakathā)

844-846. Nibbāna is called wholesome (kusala) merely by the fact of being blameless. Whatever is wholesome, all that is merely by the fact of being blameless. Therefore, it is said that Nibbāna is wholesome.

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Wholesome is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of Absolute Finality (Accantaniyāmakathā)

In saying 'relying on the Sutta: "One who has once sunk remains sunk"', the opponent thinks that the emphasis (avadhāraṇa) 'remains sunk', which was made with reference to the impossibility of supramundane faith etc. arising in that life, was made with reference to being a stump in Saṃsāra. Thinking thus, the opponent says, 'There is absolute finality for a worldling (puthujjana),' considering that there is certain wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) and that this certain wrong view is the absolute finality of a worldling.

The arising of doubt (vicikicchā) and the arising of another kind of certainty (niyāma) should be understood, after investigation, as factors that prevent absolute finality.

## End of the Commentary on the Discussion of Absolute Finality.

## 6. Ñāṇakathāvaṇṇanā

'Pariññeyya' (to be fully understood) is a term indicating the preliminary stage of the path (pubbabhāga), and 'pariññāta' (fully understood) is a term indicating the subsequent stage (aparabhāga). As for the knowledge of the truths (saccajñāṇa), since it occurs even at the moment of the path (maggakkhaṇa) by way of accomplishing functions such as full understanding, it is said to be "together with the preliminary and subsequent stages."

## 7. Commentary on the Discussion of the Dhamma (Dhammakathāvaṇṇanā)

887-888. In the Dhammakathā, regarding the Pali "rūpaṭṭhato aññassa rūpassa abhāvā": that which is called the nature of change (the essence of matter) is said to be the fixed nature (niyāma) of matter. There is no such thing as the nature of change of matter that is distinct from matter itself. Therefore, matter is not a nature other than the nature of change of matter. Thus, matter is only the nature of change; it does not have the nature of feeling (vedanā) and so on. With this intention, it should be said that "matter is fixed by the nature of matter" (rūpaṃ rūpaṭṭhena niyataṃ). It should not be said otherwise, meaning it is not fixed by a nature of matter that is distinct from the matter itself—this is the intention of the Commentator.

In that passage "rūpaṭṭhato aññassa rūpassa abhāvā" etc., when it is shown that there is no nature of change of matter distinct from matter, it is as good as showing that there is no matter distinct from the nature of change of matter. Therefore, desiring to show precisely the absence of a nature of change distinct from matter, he said "rūpasabhāvo hi" etc.

"Esa vohāro" means: the nature of matter is 'rūpasabhāva', the essence of matter is 'rūpaṭṭha'. These terms, 'rūpasabhāva' and 'rūpaṭṭha', which are used as if taking them to be distinct, are for the purpose of making known that such a nature is indeed different and distinct from feeling (vedanā) and so on.

"Tasmā" means: because matter is not distinct from the essence of matter (rūpaṭṭha). The statement of the Sakavādin (proponent), who says "matter is fixed by the nature of matter" instead of directly saying "matter is only matter, it does not have the nature of feeling etc.," is also faulty in the manner already stated. If it is faulty, why is it accepted? If it is asked thus: because the statement "matter is fixed by the nature of matter" should be said with the intention that "matter is only the nature of change, it does not have the nature of feeling etc."; therefore, when it is said, the meaning should be noted that he accepts the proposition "matter is fixed by the nature of matter."

If it is objected: "This statement 'matter is fixed by the nature of matter' is said by oneself (the Sakavādin) and not by another (the Paravādin); therefore, is it not improper to say he 'accepts' it?"—it is not so; it is proper to say so because one speaks of oneself as if speaking of another. Alternatively, in the word "vattabbaṃ," it means it should be said by the Sakavādin. If that Sakavādin should say it and if he accepts this meaning, then this is the very meaning already stated as to why the Sakavādin accepts it.

"Atthantaravasena" means: because the opponent (Paravādin) made an objection by concealing the proper reason already stated in the commentary—that "matter is only matter, it does not have the nature of feeling etc."—he (the Commentator) shows that very reason and prevents the objection. "Ito aññathā" means: apart from the mere nature of matter etc., there is no "fixed" (niyata) thing as imagined by that person (the Paravādin).

## 9. Commentary on the Discussion of the Unperfected

917-918. In the passage "na aniccādibhāvaṃ," because this matter (rūpa) has an inherent nature such as impermanence, that matter is called "aniccādibhāva." The commentator, by saying "na kevalañhi paṭhamasaccameva dukkhaṃ," shows that the question "dukkhaññeva parinipphannaṃ" is asked with reference to the truth of suffering (dukkha-sacca). This being so, that proponent (Sakavādin) should not say "cakkhāyatanaṃ aparinipphannaṃ" etc. Because states such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana) are neither non-grasped (anupādinna) states nor supramundane (lokuttara) states that are not included in the truth of suffering. "Taṃ" means "only suffering is perfected (parinipphanna), but matter is not"; because matter is also suffering, the meaning is "O friend, it should not be said."

## The Commentary on the Discussion of the Unperfected is finished.
